title: Multicellular signaling in reverse cardiac remodeling revealed by integrated bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics
authors: Steier, M.; Rivero-Garcia, I.; Flores, R. O. R.; Deshpande, A.; Aijaz, I.; Poetzsch, J.; Nazir, S.; Talamini, M.; Ast, V.; Mossinger, K.; Dewenter, M.; Meder, B.; Leuschner, F.; Kumari, M.; Backs, J.; Rangrez, A. Y.; Saez-Rodriguez, J.; Frey, N.
abstract: Heart failure results from maladaptive multicellular remodeling triggered by sustained biomechanical stress. Although mechanical unloading can promote reverse remodeling, recovery is frequently incomplete and its mechanistic basis remains unclear. Using a reversible murine pressure-overload model combined with bulk and single-nucleus transcriptomics, we demonstrate that reverse remodeling represents an actively maintained yet constrained multicellular state. Unloading improved cardiac function and partially restored extracellular matrix and metabolic programs, whereas inflammatory and mitochondrial dysfunction signatures persisted. Cardiomyocytes and endothelial cells largely re-established homeostatic transcriptional states, while fibroblasts retained activated programs that dominated residual pathology. Multicellular factor analysis delineated a reversible metabolic stress program and a persistent inflammatory-mitochondrial program coordinated across cardiac cell types. Cell-cell communication analysis identified lymphatic endothelial cells as key instructive regulators of recovery. Notably, lymphatic-derived Reelin (RELN) directly suppressed pathological fetal gene activation in murine and human cardiomyocytes, uncovering a previously unrecognized lymphoangiocrine mechanism that constrains myocardial recovery in chronic heart failure.

title: Network modeling identifies vitamin B2 control of AIFM2 deficit-driven hepatocyte death in MASLD
authors: Weihs, J.; Baldo, F.; Cardinali, A.; Youssef, G.; Ludwik, K.; Haep, N.; Tang, P.; Kumar, P.; Engelmann, C.; Quach, S.; Meindl, M.; Kucklick, M.; Engelmann, S.; Chilian, B.; Rothe, M.; Lurje, I.; Hammerich, L.; Romeike, M.; Ramachandran, P.; Kendall, T. J.; Fallowfield, J. A.; Vallier, L.; Stachelscheid, H.; Sauer, I.; Tacke, F.; Bufler, P.; Hudert, C.; Han, N.; Rezvani, M.; Takebe, T.
abstract: Drug discovery for metabolic dysfunction-associated steatotic liver disease (MASLD) remains difficult due to network effects. We developed MetaLiver, a public resource to identify druggable nodes within complex interactomes. It incorporates a MASLD-specific knowledge graph that improves bioactive compound contextualization while reducing computing time 18.8-fold. Layering progression-resolved bulk and hepatocyte-specific single-cell MASLD data onto this graph identified the vitamin B2-dependent flavoproteome (FlavProt) as an injury-sensitive network. Induced pluripotent stem cell-derived and primary human hepatocytes validated that flavin-cofactor replenishment mitigates FlavProt-dependent dysregulation, augmenting metabolic functions under cellular stress. Saturating flavin-cofactor availability blunted human immune cell activation. Clinically, a FlavProt expression score significantly correlated with poor outcomes in retrospectively stratified MASLD patients. We identified the oxidoreductase AIFM2 from this score and established experimentally that its injury-associated deficit causes hepatocyte death yet is controllable by flavin-cofactor availability. This study reveals the FlavProt as critical yet modifiable in MASLD and establishes MetaLiver for network discovery.

title: A dynamic displacement mechanism drives protein import into mitochondria
authors: Sucec, I.; Guillerm, U.; Schneider, J.; Ganesan, I.; Webling, N.; Kapitonova, A.; Steiert, C.; Schmelter, F.; Feignier, A.; Singh, R.; Fielden, L. F.; Dung, J.; Rapaport, D.; Bersch, B.; Busch, K. B.; Dehez, F.; Wiedemann, N.; Schanda, P.
abstract: Most mitochondrial proteins are produced in the cytosol and imported through the translocase of the outer mitochondrial membrane (TOM) to reach their final destination. Although this protein entry gate has been structurally characterized, it remains unclear how precursor proteins are handed off from the cytosolic receptor domains to the translocation pore. Here we show that the cytosolic domain of Tom22 - traditionally viewed as the central TOM receptor - acts not as a structured scaffold but as a largely disordered, flexible segment that plays an active role in precursor transfer. Atomic-level structural techniques and in vivo experiments identified a conserved short linear motif that forms a transient -helical element within this disordered domain. By binding to the canonical precursor protein binding sites of the receptors Tom20 and Tom70, this critical -helical segment acts as a precursor protein displacement element (PPDE). This competitive interaction facilitates the release of preproteins directly above the import pore, and thereby drives translocation across the outer mitochondrial membrane. These findings reveal that flexibility, rather than rigid structure, underlies the central transfer step of mitochondrial outer-membrane protein translocation. Our results point to a versatile mechanism for ligand displacement in chaperone, receptor, and transport systems that must balance selective binding with efficient release.

title: Dynamic Hierarchical Interleaved Bloom Filter: An Updatable Index for Large-Scale Fast Sequence Search
authors: Seiler, E.; Willemsen, M.; Piro, V. C.; Reinert, K.
abstract: Motivation: A continued decrease in sequencing costs has facilitated the exponential increase in available sequencing data, with public databases like the European Nucleotide Archive (ENA) and Sequence Read Archive (SRA) reaching well in the order of petabases. This has been the incentive to develop more scalable tools for common bioinformatics tasks. One such task is the approximate searching of short sequence patterns like genes or reads in reference data sets. In recent years, a variety of indexing data structures have been proposed for searching large sequencing databases. The state-of-the-art index, the Hierarchical Interleaved Bloom Filter (HIBF), was first-in-class to index one million samples. However, its static design necessitates costly full reconstructions as repositories grow, motivating an extension to support dynamic updates. Results: In this paper, we introduce a scalable and updatable sequence-search index by extending the HIBF with partial rebuilding to support efficient updates. We demonstrate the Dynamic HIBF's capacity for large-scale data by iteratively creating an index from over 100 TB of compressed reads across more than 39,000 full human RNA-Seq samples, updated in consecutive batches of 100. To benchmark against state-of-the-art tools, we evaluated incremental performance on a subset of 5,000 samples sub-sampled to 1% of their original read depth. In this comparative setting, the dynamic HIBF completed the sequential insertion of all 5,000 samples in 5.3 hours--23 to 42 times faster than competing methods and twice as fast as the static HIBF.

title: Interpersonal alignment in infra-slow EEG rhythms and bodily signals anticipates mutual recognition
authors: Gravel, N.; Guendelman, S.; Vidaurre, D.
abstract: Across multiple timescales, neural rhythms coordinate cognitive and physiological processes. Slower rhythms are increasingly recognised as the scale at which autonomic and interoceptive processes are folded into ongoing cognition, a brain&body view of allostatic regulation that is particularly relevant to social interaction. Examining these slow components of the electroencephalogram (EEG) during real-time interaction remains challenging. Here, we recorded infra-slow EEG alongside respiratory, cardiac and skin conductance signals during the perceptual crossing experiment, a social interaction and EEG hyperscanning paradigm. We assessed interpersonal alignment by contrasting trials in which dyads achieved mutual recognition with trials in which they did not, which separates genuine social alignment or recognition from a shared anticipatory context. Dyads achieving mutual recognition showed enhanced inter-participant alignment of 0.1 Hz infra-slow EEG power relative to those that did not, after accounting for the premovement motor potential. Alignment also differed between these trials in respiratory depth, the cardiac vagal index and skin conductance. These findings suggest that infra-slow EEG rhythms around 0.1 Hz may provide a temporal scaffold for the interpersonal coordination of brain and body, and could serve as markers for investigating the coupled processes underlying shared understanding and mutual recognition.

title: Spatiospectral signatures of stomach-brain synchrony
authors: Berther, T.; Saltafossi, M.; Fehring, J.; Rebollo, I.; Kluger, D. S.
abstract: While cognitive neuroscience has increasingly recognized the brain-body connection, the temporal dynamics of how the stomach's intrinsic rhythm (~0.05 Hz) modulates human neural activity remain poorly understood. Leveraging high-resolution magneto- encephalography (MEG) and novel high-density electrogastrography (EGG), we provide the first comprehensive spatiotemporal mapping of human gastric-brain coupling at rest. Our circular-linear correlation approach revealed widespread, broadband phase-amplitude coupling between the gastric rhythm and spontaneous cortical oscillations across delta, theta, alpha, and beta bands. Using nonnegative matrix factorization, we identified distinct spatiospectral fingerprints that significantly overlap with the known fMRI-based gastric resting-state network. Functional connectivity analyses based on multivariate Granger causality further showed that these modulation patterns extend to a gastric influence on frequency-specific, directed communication between network components. Crucially, we discovered a consistent preferred gastric phase for these modulations, i.e. during the transition between stomach waves, that was stable across brain regions, frequencies, connections, and time. These findings suggest that the gastric rhythm - potentially in unison with other physiological signals - provides a stable, global scaffold for large-scale oscillatory brain organization. By unravelling these spectral signatures, our results establish the stomach as a critical driver of the temporal coordination of human brain dynamics.

title: Spreading depolarization, not seizure activity, drives immediate early gene expression in mouse cortex after electroconvulsive stimulation
authors: Ladret, H. J.; Lupori, L.; Sieni, L.; Stroukov, E.; Kanamori, T.; Ulrich, S.; Schneider, E.; Deuring, G.; Bruhl, A. B.; Keller, G. B.
abstract: Electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) is a highly effective treatment for several psychiatric disorders, though its biological mechanisms remain unclear. ECT's therapeutic action has traditionally been attributed to the generalized seizure it induces. However, this view is challenged by the recent finding that electroconvulsive stimulation (ECS) can trigger a spreading depolarization (SD) in cortex. Because SD drives massive molecular changes, including expression of the plasticity-related immediate early gene Fos, we hypothesized that SD could be a key mediator of ECT's plasticity-inducing effects. We recorded the neuronal response to ECS in mouse dorsal cortex and observed similar activity to that of patients undergoing ECT. SD, rather than the seizure activity, accounted for increased Fos expression in mouse dorsal cortex. SD was also associated with EEG features that predict positive treatment outcome of ECT in patients. Our results suggest that the therapeutic efficacy of ECT may be mediated by SD and imply that a currently unmonitored neurophysiological event may serve as a relevant biomarker to predict and optimize ECT outcomes.

title: Decoding Articulatory and Phonetic Features: Somatotopic and Sensorimotor Representations in Native and Non-native Consonant Perception
authors: Tseng, T.; Thibault, S.; Krzonowski, J.; Canault, M.; Roy, A.; Brozzoli, C.; Boulenger, V.
abstract: Speech perception relies on the integration of auditory and articulatory information, yet the precise role of motor regions remains debated. We combined fMRI with multivariate pattern analyses (MVPA) and behavioral measures to investigate cortical representations of native French and non-native Mandarin consonant perception under clear and noisy conditions. Cross-modal classification analysis showed that articulator-specific features of perceived degraded native bilabial and dental consonants are mapped somatotopically in right lip and tongue motor areas, which are also engaged in consonant production. These representations may support consonant categorization by compensating for degraded auditory input. Representational similarity analysis further revealed that a network encompassing bilateral temporal auditory and frontal motor regions encodes phonetic features, including place and manner of articulation, for both native and non-native consonants. Our findings demonstrate that speech perception is inherently sensorimotor and that motor regions support both low-level embodied articulator-specific mapping and higher-level phonetic feature representations.

title: The bile acid receptor TGR5 is a modulator of the bone marrow microenvironment
authors: Alonso-Calleja, A.; Perino, A.; Schyrr, F.; Ferreira Lopes, S.; Delitsikou, V.; Jalil, A.; Kettenberger, U.; Galavotti, M. C.; Martins, A.; Bataclan, C.; Pioletti, D. P.; Schoonjans, K.; Naveiras, O.
abstract: The gut is an emerging regulator of bone marrow (BM) hematopoiesis, with several molecules involved in this communication. Among them, bile acids (BAs) act as a relay between the microbiota and the rest of the body by activating specific receptors, including Takeda G protein-coupled receptor 5 (TGR5). Although TGR5 has potent regulatory effects in immune cells, its role in the BM remains unclear. Here, we show that TGR5 is expressed across hematopoietic populations, including hematopoietic stem and progenitor cells. While TGR5 deficiency did not affect steady-state hematopoiesis, it mildly impaired cell-autonomous short-term hematopoietic reconstitution. In contrast, TGR5 deletion altered the BM microenvironment. Young male, but not female, Tgr5-/- mice showed reduced bone marrow adipose tissue (BMAT) alongside an accumulation of BM adipocyte progenitors, consistent with impaired progenitor differentiation. TGR5 deficiency also blunted BMAT expansion during obesity and aging, with reduced myeloid-lymphoid progenitor ratios in male mice. Together, our results indicate that TGR5 contributes to sex-dependent regulation of BM adiposity and identify it as a potential target for modulating the BM niche.

title: Identification of a somatic H3K23me3 methyltransferase SET-19 in C. elegans
authors: Xu, M.; Fan, Z.; Yan, C.; Chen, X.; Huang, X.; Zhu, C.; Hong, M.; Cheng, J.; Hou, X.; Li, S.; Li, M.; Zhao, Z.; Shi, Y.; Huang, M.; Guang, S.; Feng, X.
abstract: Histone methylation plays essential roles in modulating chromatin organization and gene expression. H3K23 methylation is a conserved histone modification, yet its biological roles and the enzymes responsible for its deposition remain poorly understood. Here, we show that the loss of set-19 leads to a pronounced reduction in H3K23 methylation in C. elegans, as revealed by quantitative mass spectrometry, western blotting, and immunofluorescence staining. In vitro biochemical assays show that recombinant SET-19 proteins purified from E. coli directly catalyze H3K23 methylation. Genome-wide chromatin immunoprecipitation assays reveal that H3K23me3 is enriched at heterochromatic regions and that loss of set-19 alters H3K23me3 levels, accompanied by derepression of a subset of genes. Genetic analyses indicate that SET-19 is dispensable for both germline and somatic RNAi as well as transgenerational epigenetic inheritance of RNAi. SET-19 is predominantly expressed in somatic cells and specifically mediates H3K23me3 deposition in somatic tissues. The loss of set-19 causes a modest developmental delay. Together, our results identify SET-19 as a somatic H3K23 methyltransferase and link SET-19-dependent H3K23me3 to transcriptional repression in C. elegans.

title: Can Folding Models Tell Binders from Bluffers? Evidence from POISK: The Patent-Derived Antibody Dataset
authors: Tupikina, D.; Roncoli, A.; Bujotzek, A.; Abanades, B.
abstract: Structure prediction models are increasingly deployed as zero-shot digital screens in antibody design, operating under the assumption that high folding confidence implies true binding. However, rigorous validation of this premise has been limited by small test sets, narrow target diversity, and the risk of data leakage from training-adjacent structures. Here we introduce POISK: Patent-extracted Organization of Immunoglobulin Sequence Knowledge, a large-scale dataset derived from the US patent literature, comprising 89074 antibody-antigen records extracted from 10110 patents using an LLM-based pipeline. From this resource, we curate a balanced benchmark set of 22494 complexes: 11247 patent-validated binders without a known resolved structure paired with putative non-binders constructed from sequence-similar human repertoire antibodies. Using this dataset, we benchmark six leading structure prediction models (AlphaFold-Multimer, Boltz-2, IntelliFold v2, OpenFold3, Protenix-v1, and Protenix-v2) on their ability to discriminate binders from decoys. The best-performing model, Protenix-v2, achieves 72% pairwise accuracy over all pairs and 87% on the most confident half of predictions, and correctly identifies the true binder from a pool of 50 candidates in 29% of trials; this represents a substantial enrichment over random selection, yet remains far from reliable single-candidate identification. Structural consensus across models also discriminates binders from decoys, with pairwise accuracy reaching 73.1% when three or more models converge on a pose (DockQ>0.23, covering around 54.2% of pairs). Epitope localization remains unreliable: the best model contacts annotated epitope residues in only 62.8% of cases, indicating that binding discrimination does not establish accurate epitope localization. Our results suggest that current folding models provide useful but limited signal for antibody screening and should be complemented by orthogonal methods. We release POISK as a community resource for future benchmarking and model training.

title: CellChat Hotspot: A Targeted Approach to Cell Cell Communication Analysis With Spatial transcriptomics Validation.
authors: Monaco, D.; Dioguardi, M.; Dipalma, M.; Mattioli, E.; Zito, F. A.; Giovannelli, F.; Ricco, A.; Brunetti, O.; Argentiero, A.; De Summa, S.
abstract: Abstract. In recent years, single cell RNA sequencing (scRNA seq) has enabled the investigation of intercellular communication through Cell Cell Communication (CCC) tools such as CellChat. Despite their potential, these approaches remain challenging to interpret, particularly when global analyses generate complex interaction networks that may include biologically irrelevant signals. To address this limitation, we developed a framework termed CellChat Hotspot, designed to improve the biological interpretability of inferred communication networks. This approach integrates gene set enrichment analysis with a context driven filtering strategy, selecting both genes and cells based on their functional relevance prior to communication inference. Applied to stage II colon cancer data, CellChat Hotspot enabled the identification of condition-specific interaction patterns associated with recurrence. Non recurrent patients showed enrichment of immune related processes, whereas recurrent cases were characterized by pathways associated with invasion and metastasis. Notably, a loss of interaction in the HSPG pathway between CALB1+ and stromal cells was observed in recurrent patients, suggesting a potential disruption of cell matrix adhesion mechanisms. To verify the reliability of this finding, we applied the framework to spatial transcriptomics data, which confirmed the presence of the HSPG2 DAG1 interaction in non-recurrent tumors and its near absence in recurrent ones. Overall, this framework provides a biologically guided strategy for studying intercellular communication in complex systems such as the tumor microenvironment.

title: Acute FMR1 reduction alters cellular and circuit properties in human cortex
authors: Singh, A.; Abbaspoor, S.; Chung, L.; Heinrich, M. J.; Stone, S.; Lidov, H.; Maio, B.; Tran, T. P.; Yoon, J.; Teng, J.; Reyes, C. M.; Hammarlund, E.; Xu, X.; Hirsh, R.; Guardado, R.; Buttermore, E.; Rotenberg, A.; Gavornik, J.; Ferguson, B.; Farrell, J. S.; Osterweil, E. K.
abstract: Transcriptional silencing of FMR1 results in Fragile X syndrome (FXS), the leading inherited cause of intellectual disability (ID) and autism. Although the impact of FMR1 reduction on cortical function has been studied using the Fmr1-/y mouse model, mechanistic insights from the human brain are lacking. Here we show that acute FMR1 reduction in ex vivo human cortical slices induces transcriptomic changes that are concordant with those observed in FXS patient cortex, identifying many targets not altered in the Fmr1-/y mouse model. Consistent with changes in ion channel expression specifically in human tissue, FMR1 reduction drives increased intrinsic excitability of deep-layer pyramidal neurons and network-level population bursts observed with two-photon calcium imaging. Together, these findings define the consequences of FMR1 loss in human cortex and establish an experimental framework for identifying human-specific mechanisms and therapeutic targets relevant to FXS.

title: Distinct contemplative traditions share a common EEG complexity signature
authors: Shrimali, P.; Sasidharan, A.; Malipeddi, S.; Ventura, B.; Venugopal, R.; Nair, A. K.; Tewarie, P. K. B.; Nagendra, R. P.; Kutty, B. M.; Northoff, G.
abstract: Meditation encompasses diverse practices that train attention inward, unlike externally oriented task states. Which brain-activity features are shared across contemplative practices, which accompany long-term training, and which are tradition-specific remains unclear. We leveraged electroencephalography data from 226 participants: advanced meditators of four contemplative traditions and non-meditating controls. We developed a neurodynamic profiling approach spanning 21 features across four feature families: oscillatory, aperiodic, complexity and timescale. Using extensive machine learning, we found that meditation and task states were reliably separable, driven by a large, uniform drop in complexity during meditation. Meditators differed from controls primarily in timescale dynamics. Traditions exhibited distinct signatures in all feature families except complexity, and meditators neurodynamic profiles identified the contemplative tradition they practiced. A classifier trained on three traditions could still detect meditation in the fourth, regardless of which tradition was left out, relying mainly on complexity features. Diverse contemplative techniques therefore converge on a shared neurodynamic signature - reduced complexity during meditation relative to an external task, that generalizes across traditions. This shared signature coexists with tradition-specific profiles in oscillatory, aperiodic, and timescale features.

title: Measuring satellite arrays of the human Y chromosome from sequencing reads
authors: Ortigas-Vasquez, A.; Guarracino, A.
abstract: Human Y chromosome satellites vary widely but remain difficult to measure in large cohorts. We developed Yruler, which uses pangenome assemblies to measure satellite lengths, composition and Y dosage from sequencing reads without alignment. Across cohorts, we find lineage-associated differences in centromere and non-centromeric array length, and show that heterochromatin components vary unequally within lineages. Yruler enables population-scale studies of how Y satellite variation relates to health and disease.

title: CNVSIM: an interpretable cross-study copy-number reference atlas for cancer subtyping
authors: YU, J.; Bardet-Trouilloud, J.; Jaeger, S.; Baudis, M.
abstract: Genome-wide copy-number variation (CNV) profiles provide a representation of structural changes in cancer genomes, but interpreting new profiles with respect to their underlying biology remains challenging. We developed CNVSIM, which organizes CNV profiles into root-specific reference spaces and defines subtypes with chromosome-scale and gene-level signatures. Applied to the Progenetix dataset, CNVSIM established 112 CNV-defined subtypes across 19 cancer roots, supported by 155,881 neoplastic analyses from diverse studies and assay platforms. In the context of diagnostic concepts, these subtypes distinguish genomic architectures and reveal associated differences in somatic mutation patterns, with selected associations supported across cohorts. In practice, CNVSIM enables new profiles to be projected onto the established reference and linked to corresponding reference analyses. Additionally, CNVSIM enables the identification of cancer cell lines with copy-number architectures similar to individual subtypes, while also revealing gaps in subtype and alteration coverage based on available data. Reference robustness was supported by subtype recovery after data reduction and assignment of 77.6% of held-out TCGA profiles using a reference reconstructed without TCGA.

title: pH-driven dynamics and mechanisms of LNP-mediated siRNA delivery
authors: Hossain, K. A.; Valerio, M.; Medina, P.; Souza, P. C. T.; Orozco, M.
abstract: We present a comprehensive analysis of a clinically relevant DLin-MC3-DMA (MC3)-based lipid nanoparticle (LNP) formulation that exhibits strong short interfering RNA (siRNA, ~21 nt) delivery and potent inhibition of targeted RNAs. Using a combination of coarse-grained and atomistic molecular dynamics simulations, we characterize the pH-dependent structure of both unloaded and siRNA-loaded LNPs, elucidate the mechanism of siRNA encapsulation, and use these models to propose a plausible mechanism of endosomal escape. Consistent with prior experimental and computational studies, our simulations reproduce an inverted-hexagonal-type morphology in a ~70 nm siRNA-loaded LNPs. For the smaller LNPs mimetics, with only one siRNA sequence, we observe a similar hydrated core as observed in the larger 70 nm LNP model. Such hydrated channel provides a polar environment suitable for accommodating RNA, whose charge is neutralized mainly by the MC3 ionizable lipids that remain protonated near the RNA even at high pH, thereby bridging the RNA with the surrounding lipid environment. This structural picture is also consistently observed across our multiscale simulations, with smaller self-assembled LNP mimetics reproducing the same local organization at both coarse-grained and atomistic resolution. A potential mechanism of endosomal escape, emerges spontaneously from the simulations, involving stalk formation between the LNP and the endosomal membrane, followed by the opening of a water-filled pore that permits slow siRNA diffusion, in line with the low efficiency and slow kinetics reported for endosomal escape. The rate-limiting step of endosomal escape arises from persistent electrostatic coupling between RNA and protonated MC3 ionizable lipids maintained by the immediate RNA-lipid environment, hindering cargo disengagement even after pore formation. This delayed release is consistent with the experimentally observed time-dependent inhibitory activity of the loaded LNP. Together, these results highlight the importance of local pKa; and protonation effects near the RNA, which are not captured by global apparent pKa; measurements.

title: A general method for bootstrapping dense 3D segmentations from sparse 2D annotations
authors: Thiyagarajan, V. V.; Sheridan, A.; Harris, K. M.; Manor, U.
abstract: Volumetric electron microscopy (vEM) provides unparalleled insight into cellular architecture, transforming our understanding of fundamental biological processes. Precise quantification of volumetric bioimaging data requires 3D instance segmentation, but the time and cost of manual ground-truth annotation present a major bottleneck for training accurate machine learning models. Our lightweight two-stage method generates complete 3D instance segmentations from sparse 2D annotations. A 2D network predicts dense boundaries on every section from minimal 2D labels. A 3D network pre- trained on synthetic data infers connectivity between sections. Across the imaging modalities and biological structures tested, our method generates base segmentations with minutes of human effort per volume. Models trained on these 2D [->] 3D pseudo ground-truth segmentations approach the accuracy of fully supervised models while reducing human annotation time by four orders of magnitude. This method does not require dense 3D labeling and thus democratizes scalable volumetric analysis across imaging modalities in basic science and biomedical applications.

title: Synaptic pruning, myelination and the emergence of psychiatric disorders in late adolescence
authors: Averbeck, B. B.; Brunel, N.
abstract: Adolescence is an important developmental period during which there are diverse changes in the brain and behavior. Goal-directed behaviors, including working memory, response inhibition, and reinforcement learning, improve during adolescence. At the same time there is substantial pruning of excitatory connections in prefrontal cortex and ongoing myelination of axons, which likely underlie these improvements in behavior. However, psychiatric disorders also become increasingly prevalent in late adolescence. In this study, we develop computational models that suggest a hypothesis for how ongoing changes in the brain can give rise to the increased prevalence of psychiatric disorders including depression, obsessive-compulsive disorder (OCD), schizophrenia and substance use disorders (SUDs). We show that both myelination and pruning during adolescence lead to attractor landscapes in which strongly encoded memories, embedded in patterns of synaptic connectivity, come to dominate brain activity. Pruning and myelination lead to large, strong dynamical attractors which, if they are related to aversive emotions, can drive intrusive thoughts and compulsions in OCD, rumination in depression, or if they are related to drug exposure, compulsive drug seeking in SUDs. Thus, we suggest that psychiatric disorders emerge when early experience embeds pathophysiological patterns of synaptic connectivity in neural circuits. The neural changes during adolescent development then cause these memories to inflexibly dominate the neural and behavioral landscape.

title: Assessing multi-eGO Predictions of PDZ2-Peptide Binding across Mutations
authors: Ardizzone, C.; Stegani, B.; Bacic Toplek, F.; Gianni, S.; Capelli, R.; Camilloni, C.
abstract: Accurately predicting how mutations alter protein-peptide binding remains challenging for molecular simulations because both conformational sampling and binding kinetics are computationally demanding. Here, we investigate whether multi-eGO, a hybrid transferable/structure-based atomistic-resolution model previously developed and validated for protein-small molecule interactions, can be transferred to protein-peptide binding. Using the PDZ2 domain of protein tyrosine phosphatase basophil-like in complex with the peptide EQVTAV as a benchmark, we show that multi-eGO, calibrated on explicit-solvent simulations of the complex, predicts the equilibrium dissociation constant of the complex within the expected uncertainty, although binding and unbinding are both accelerated by several orders of magnitude. We then introduce conservative mutations in PDZ2 and in the peptide without additional training for each mutant. For the PDZ2 mutants in complex with EQVTAV, the predicted dissociation constants follow experiment (Pearson r = 0.97), with a compressed response, whereas smaller effects, such as that of the peptide mutation and the coupling between peptide and protein mutations, are not re-solved. A maximum-caliber reweighting of the simulated first-passage times shows that a single acceleration factor, common to all twelve complexes, accounts for most of the kinetic discrepancy, and that the remaining system-specific errors in the rate constants are recovered by reweighting the simulated events. Up to a global time scale, the binding and unbinding events sampled by multi-eGO are thus consistent with the experimental kinetics. These results define multi-eGO as a computationally efficient approach to estimate the effects of conservative protein mutations on peptide binding affinity and to inter-pret the associated kinetics, while absolute rate constants remain out of reach.

title: Network modularity reveals context and state-dependent reorganization of time-varying functional connectivity in single-cell resolved neural activity recordings
authors: Moon, S.; Liang, J.; Lee, H. J.; Maalouf, A.; Yu, Z.; Moza, S.; Zhang, Y.; Lu, H.
abstract: An important goal of neuroscience is to understand how biological neural networks organize activity at multiple scales to enable complex information processing and behavioral output. To address this challenge, large-scale neural activity datasets with increased resolution and wider coverage have become more prevalent across many model systems. However, bridging the gap in scale between changes in pairwise functional connectivity between neurons and changes in brain-wide organization of activity remains a key challenge. In this work, we demonstrate application of modularity-based community detection and network modularity to single-cell resolved recordings, for the first time, as a method to summarize complex changes in time-varying functional connectivity, facilitating comparisons across multiple time windows, recordings, and conditions. We apply these methods to both single-cell resolved multi-cell and whole-brain activity recordings. In the multi-cell recordings, we find that food odor changes functional connectivity between existing network modules in a C. elegans locomotory interneuron network, rather than reorganizing them. In spontaneous whole-brain activity, we identify several key hub neurons and combinations that significantly destabilize module assignments when silenced. Together, these results demonstrate community detection and modularity as a method for detecting context and network state-dependent changes in functional connectivity at the intermediate scale of network modules in single-cell resolved neural activity. Results from these analyses facilitate future investigation of mechanisms that mediate organization of neural activity at intermediate scales.

title: Reactive and predictive processes during unpredictable driving collisions in virtual reality: an exploratory immersive study with multimodal neurophysiological monitoring
authors: Cannard, C.; Yesilbas, D.
abstract: Anticipatory neurophysiological activity before unpredictable emotional events has been reported for decades, but the effects are small, difficult to replicate, and obtained almost exclusively in stripped-down laboratory paradigms. Whether they reflect genuine predictive processes or methodological artifacts remains debated; one rarely tested possibility is that such settings mute it. We examined anticipation in an immersive virtual reality (VR) driving simulation whose collision outcomes were assigned by a quantum random number generator, while EEG, photoplethysmography (PPG), EMG, EOG and inertial (IMU) signals were recorded from a single wireless dry-electrode headset built into the VR display. Sixteen participants passively observed 120 driving sequences ending in a collision or no collision. Length-matched pre- and post-stimulus windows were analysed identically with mass-univariate hierarchical general linear models under permutation cluster correction, plus machine-learning classification across held-out participants. Two post-stimulus clusters differentiated the conditions, the largest peaking at 451.6 ms (d = -1.35), with broadband power modulation robust to baseline modelling, decoded from held-out participants with up to 93.8% accuracy. No time-domain effect or decodable information preceded stimulus onset, but a broadband spectral difference did, surviving preregistered controls for expectation bias (run length), time-on-task build-up and ocular or facial-muscle artifact: directionally consistent in 13 of 15 participants, with pre- and post-stimulus power coupled in all 16. Heart rate differentiated the conditions neither alone nor when added to the classifier. The study was preregistered; the BIDS-format data, analysis code and an open-source EEGLAB plugin are publicly available.

title: Immersive display systems for simulating natural vision
authors: Katti, H.; Murphy, A. P.; Helde, M.; Deshpande, H.; Lee, T. J.; Knight, R.; Gregg, C.; Solinas, C.; Cameron, K.; Bandy, D.; Dold, G.; Leopold, D. A.
abstract: Vision is traditionally studied using simplified stimuli presented briefly near the center of a flat display while subjects maintain visual fixation. This paradigm contrasts sharply with real-world vision, which is immersive, dynamic and strongly influenced by self-initiated actions. Traditional approaches have allowed researchers to systematically study the neural encoding of visual features and the influence of cognitive operations such as attention. However, other methods are needed to study more holistic and first-person perspectives on vision, such as those related to physical space, continuous time, and self-movement. To enable the study of these and other aspects of real-world vision, we developed hemispherical ("dome") display systems for macaque visual neuroscience. For functional MRI experiments, a compact rear-projection dome display fits within the bore of a clinical MRI scanner. For electrophysiological recordings, a larger front-projection dome display is illuminated from above using a spherical mirror. Both setups complete and dynamic stimulation of approximately 180 degrees of the subject's field of view, thus facilitating studies requiring visual immersion. To ensure accurate angular geometry across the hemispherical display, we present unified rendering and calibration software that supports natural fisheye videos, conventional visual stimuli, and virtual 3D environments. The calibration procedure automatically compensates for projector, mirror, and dome distortions through geometric pre-warping, ensuring correct visual-angle representation across the display. Pilot fMRI experiments demonstrate robust activation of peripheral visual cortex during both conventional pattern stimulation and naturalistic self-movement. Together, these dome systems provide a flexible platform for investigating aspects of vision that are difficult to study with conventional displays, including peripheral processing, visual immersion, optic flow, self-motion, and holistic scene perception.
